newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Stg to ease but no boost for UK trade.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Stg to ease but no boost for UK trade.

text.p: Sterling's robust rally could come a cropper as British growth weakens in 1998 and investors take their cash elsewhere, a Reuters survey showed on Monday.
An average of 27 analysts, canvassed between April 7 and 9, saw sterling at around 1.6000 dollars by end-June. Against the German mark, 24 analysts put sterling at 2.7500.
By end-1998, analysts predicted the pound would stand at 1.5800 dollars and 2.5000 marks, the average forecasts showed.

"With weaker prospects in 1998, there is likely to be capital outflows from sterling. Other equity markets around the world will look more attractive so the direction of portfolio investment will become strongly negative for the UK and for sterling," said Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking.
On April 9, the last day of the poll, sterling closed at 1.6240 dollars and 2.7825 marks.
Sterling currently is buoyed by the prospect of higher interest rates in Britain.
But analysts believe that once base rates are raised, there will be little incentive for investors to stay with the pound.
Reuters surveys show that most economists expect a modest rise in base rates from the current six percent, no matter which party wins the May 1 election.
"When rate increases have been made, the argument for buying sterling comes to an end," said Trevor Williams, economist at Lloyds TSB.
He also predicted that with growth easing off in Britain in 1998 and European economies faring better, investors would have another reason for selling sterling.
But while some analysts expect both sterling and the dollar to be strong in 1997, a topping out of interest rates in the United States could mean cable regains some of its strength in 1998.
Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at Bank of America, saw sterling reaching 1.6600 dollars by end-1998.

Nevertheless, the overall picture of softer sterling, while a welcome relief for British businesses who have seen exports hit and imports benefiting from a strong currency, is not expected to bring Britain's trade deficit down.
Twenty-three analysts forecast a 13.5 billion sterling trade deficit in 1997, widening to 15.9 billion the following year.

"Initially, the consequence will be to push up import prices, so the improvement in the trade balance... will not come immediately, but by the second half of 1998 I would think the volume effects would become dominant and we should see an improvement in the trade balance.
"The outlook is not particularly good, but it should still improve towards tail end as continental European demand picks up," Hawkins said.
